heading: Summary
body: Add secure HMAC request authentication to ASP.NET Core APIs with lightweight, configurable middleware — or enforce it across a Kubernetes service mesh without touching application code. Requests are signed and verified against named policies . A policy carries a key pair, a hash algorithm choice, a replay window, and optionally schemes — named header sets whose values are folded into the signature. The .NET library, the mesh verifier and the TypeScript client all build the same signing content, so a request signed by any of them verifies against any of the others.

heading: Features
body: ASP.NET Core library Policy-based signing and verification — validate requests against multiple named policies. Schemes — require specific header values per policy, with automatic mapping of those headers to claims. Built-in nonce management for replay protection, in-memory or over any IDistributedCache — plus an atomic Redis cache shared between instances in the opt-in HmacManager.StackExchangeRedis package. Dynamic policies — a singleton collection, or pulled at runtime from a database or other store. First-class ASP.NET Core authentication/authorization integration, plus client-side request signing via an HttpClient handler. Structured ILogger diagnostics with stable event ids — every rejection reports which check failed, and no message can carry a private key. Targets net8.0 and net10.0 . Kubernetes / Istio Envoy/Istio ext-authz service — enforce HMAC at the ingress edge or between services (ambient waypoints); requests without a valid signature are rejected with 403 , no application changes required. HmacPolicy CRD + operator — declare policies as Kubernetes resources; the operator reconciles them into the ConfigMap and Secret the verifier mounts. Private keys sourced from Kubernetes Secrets ; policy and key changes hot-reload without a pod restart . Redis bundled for replay protection — no external dependencies to provision. Installable via Helm and indexed on Artifact Hub.

heading: .NET Library
body: HmacManager is available on NuGet. Register a policy and let the built-in authentication handler verify incoming requests: On the calling side, sign outgoing requests automatically by attaching the handler to an HttpClient : → .NET documentation — schemes, dynamic policies, HmacEvents , IConfiguration binding, custom signing content, and logging.

heading: Kubernetes (Istio ext-authz)
body: HmacManager also ships a containerized verification service and a Helm chart for enforcing HMAC authentication in a Kubernetes mesh — at the ingress edge or between services — without changing application code. The service runs as an Envoy ext-authz HTTP server: an Istio ingress gateway (north-south) or an ambient waypoint (east-west, service-to-service) calls it before forwarding a request, and anything without a valid HMAC signature is rejected with 403 . Redis is bundled for replay protection — no external dependencies to provision. Prefer GitOps? Declare policies as HmacPolicy custom resources and let the operator reconcile them into the config the verifier mounts — no --set flags required: → Kubernetes documentation — the ext-authz service, the CRD and operator, chart values, and enforcement. Helm chart — kubernetes/chart · Artifact Hub Container images — zills/hmac-manager (ext-authz service) · zills/hmac-manager-operator (policy operator) on Docker Hub

heading: JavaScript / TypeScript Client
body: hmac-manager is available on npm. Sign requests from a browser or Node client so they verify against an HmacManager -protected API — and verify incoming requests, so a Node service can be one itself without a .NET hop or a mesh sidecar. Verification needs the private key, so it belongs on a server. → Client documentation — verifying, schemes, the API surface, and where the private key can safely live.

Other ways to install With pipx or pip: Or run it without installing — the package is kx-cli , the command is kx : See the install guide for more.

heading: Usage
body: No more copying names out of kubectl get — one listing, then everything after it by number. Indexes come several at a time, as ranges, or narrowed. kubectl's own flags pass through — kx delete 3 --force --grace-period=0 , kx logs 3 -f --tail=100 . Passing -n with an index is refused, since the index already carries the namespace it was listed from. So is --context , --kubeconfig , --cluster or --server , for the cluster, and a listing taken with one prints unnumbered. Listings made with -A are indexed too, each row with its own namespace. Known kinds drop the get — kx pods , kx deploy -n kube-system — kubectl's shorthands and your CRDs included. The --watch / -w flag redraws the table in place rather than appending lines. Tab completion, from kx completion , shows the resource behind each index: kx describe offers 1 api-7d8f (Pod) , not a bare number. See the indexes guide for more.

heading: Triage a namespace
body: Bare kx diag sweeps the current namespace — every workload kind, plus Services, PVCs, Ingresses and Pods nothing owns — and ranks what's unhealthy. It reads live usage too, so a Pod running hot against its memory limit is flagged as an OOMKill risk before it dies. With an index, kx diag diagnoses a single resource: a top level verdict, a findings summary, a per-pod status table, log tails from broken containers and warning events — one screen instead of four kubectl commands. See the triage guide for more.

heading: Read a Secret in plaintext
body: The kx secret --decode command prints an indexed Secret's keys and values decoded. With --key / -k , it prints a single value raw — no banner, no wrapping — so it drops straight into a shell. Bare kx secret --decode decodes every Secret in the namespace in one call, confirming first — that prints every credential you have. See the secrets guide for more.

heading: Scan images for CVEs
body: The kx scan command scans the unique container images of an indexed workload. Bare kx scan sweeps every workload in the namespace. Results come back as a severity summary, or the full per-image CVE report with --full . Requires the CLI for the selected engine — Docker Scout by default, or Trivy and Grype via kx engine . See the scan guide for more.

heading: See what owns what
body: The kx tree command walks the ownership graph — Deployment to ReplicaSet to Pods — and indexes every tree node it draws, so anything in the tree is one number away. Bare kx tree graphs the whole namespace. See the ownership guide for more.

heading: Reports in the browser
body: The --html flag on kx diag , kx scan , kx tree , and kx top renders the same analysis as a page and opens it in your browser. It binds 127.0.0.1 only and writes nothing to disk. The page is drawn in your active theme. Sweep rows expand into that resource's full report, image rows into the CVEs behind their counts — detail the terminal has no room for. Add --out to write the page to a file instead of serving it — what you want in CI, where kx diag --out report.html is the whole command. See the browser reports guide for more.

heading: Spend an index anywhere
body: Beyond the two dozen kubectl verbs kx wraps, the kx ref command covers the rest, and every tool that isn't kubectl: it prints what an index refers to, as an argument fragment that drops straight into another command. The --name , --namespace and --kind flags print one field alone, and nothing here touches the cluster, so kx ref answers instantly even with nothing reachable. See the kx ref guide for more.

heading: Marks
body: An index is a position, and positions move — the next kx get renumbers everything out from under it. A mark is a name you choose instead, pinned to one resource, so it keeps working across every listing that comes after it. A mark survives re-listing, which is what an index cannot do. It is pinned to the cluster it was taken in, and will not resolve in another — the same name means a different resource there, or none at all. Running kx state drop --all leaves marks alone; only kx unmark --all removes them. See the marks guide for more.

heading: Use kx in CI
body: The --fail-on flag turns a sweep into a build gate, and --json prints the same analysis as a document for anything downstream. Exit 2 means findings breached the threshold, 1 means kx itself failed — so a pipeline can tell "the cluster is sick" from "the check never ran". See the CI guide for more.

heading: MCP server
body: The kx mcp command runs a Model Context Protocol server on stdio, so an agent — Claude Code, an IDE, an agent framework — reads a cluster the way you do: by kind and name, by a mark, or by an index from your current listing. The MCP tools are read-only against the cluster; mark , the one write, only adds a name to kx's own state. Start it with --write-listings and the agent's listings join your history, tagged as the agent's, so you can spend its numbers yourself — and kx warns before a mutating command does. See the agent guide for more.

heading: State and history
body: Recent kx get results are kept as a history — 10 by default, configurable — with a cursor marking the entry indexes resolve against. Each entry remembers the context it was listed in, so a staging index is never resolved against production — kx refuses and relists instead. See the state guide for more.

heading: Configuration
body: Settings live in ~/.kx/config.toml , and every one takes a KX environment override. The two worth changing have commands of their own — kx theme and kx engine both persist your choice. Styling is dropped when stdout isn't a terminal, so kx get pods grep worker stays clean. NO COLOR is honored too. See the configuration guide for more.

heading: Themes
body: The kx theme command lists the available themes with a preview of each, and kx theme persists your choice, by name or index. Eleven themes ship with it, github-dark by default. See the themes guide for more.

heading: Commands
body: Every command takes indexes from the listing kx get last produced. The command reference covers every argument and flag. All commands Command Description --- --- kx annotate [ ...] Set or remove annotations on an indexed resource. kx annotations ... Show annotations for one or more indexed resources. kx context [ ] List kubeconfig contexts, or switch to an indexed one; alias: kx contexts. kx cordon ... Mark one or more indexed Nodes unschedulable. kx cp Copy files to or from an indexed Pod via kubectl cp. kx debug [ ...] Open a debug shell on an indexed Pod (an ephemeral container, for images with no shell) or Node (a privileged Pod on the host). kx delete ... Delete one or more indexed resources (prompts for confirmation unless --yes). kx describe ... Show full kubectl describe output for one or more indexed resources. kx diagnostic [ ] Diagnose an indexed Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob, Service, PersistentVolumeClaim, Ingress, Pod, or Node, or triage a whole namespace when no index is given (-n to pick one, -A for every namespace); alias: kx diag. kx drain Evict the Pods from an indexed Node (prompts for confirmation unless --yes). kx edit Open an indexed resource in your editor via kubectl edit. kx events ... Show Kubernetes events for one or more indexed resources. kx exec [ ...] Open an interactive shell in an indexed Pod, Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet or DaemonSet (bash, falling back to sh). kx get [ ...] List resources and assign index numbers for use with other commands; shorthand: kx (e.g. kx pods, kx po 3). kx label [ ...] Set or remove labels on an indexed resource. kx labels ... Show labels for one or more indexed resources; --selector formats output as a label selector. kx logs ... Stream logs for an indexed resource; aggregates across Pods for Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and Services. kx mark [ ] [ ] Pin an indexed resource to a name that survives re-listing; with no arguments, lists marks. kx namespace [ ] List Namespaces, or switch to an indexed one; alias: kx ns. kx port-forward Forward a local port to an indexed resource (Pod, Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Service). kx ref ... Print what an index refers to, for commands kx doesn't wrap. kx rollout Run a rollout action (status, restart, pause, resume, history, undo) on a Deployment, StatefulSet, or DaemonSet. kx scale Scale an indexed Deployment, StatefulSet, or ReplicaSet to a given replica count. kx scan [ ] Scan the unique container images of an indexed workload for vulnerabilities, or a whole namespace when no index is given (-n to pick one, -A for every namespace); prints a severity summary table by default, or the raw scanner output with --full. Requires the CLI for the selected scan engine (Docker Scout by default; Trivy or Grype via --engine — see kx engine). kx secret [ ...] List Secrets like kx get, or show an indexed Secret's data with --decode; alias: kx secrets. kx set Change an indexed workload's container images with kx set image, printing each one before and after. kx taint [ ...] Set or remove taints on an indexed Node. kx top [ ] List CPU/memory usage for Pods (default) or Nodes and assign index numbers, like kx get; shows usage as a percent of limits (Pods) or capacity (Nodes) unless --no-limits. kx tree [ ] Show the ownership graph for an indexed resource or Namespace, or for the whole current namespace when no index is given (-n to pick one, -A for every namespace); assigns indexes to tree nodes by default. kx uncordon ... Mark one or more indexed Nodes schedulable again. kx unmark [ ...] Remove marks by name; --all removes every mark. kx wait ... Wait until indexed resources are ready: a Pod or Node Ready, a PVC Bound, a Job Complete, a LoadBalancer Service given an address. kx yaml ... Print the raw YAML manifest for one or more indexed resources; --show filters to specific top-level fields. kx state [ ] Show current state, jump to a history position, list all entries with --all, or expand the switch targets with --targets. kx engine [ ] List available scan engines or persist a default choice by name or index. kx theme [ ] List available color themes or persist a choice by name or index. kx mcp Serve kx's diagnostics, ownership trees, evidence and marks to AI agents over MCP (stdio). kx docs [ ] Read kx's documentation in the terminal: a topic, or the list of them. kx completion Generate a shell completion script for kx (bash, zsh, fish, powershell).

heading: Follow a session
body: Keep it open in a second terminal next to claude , and every prompt, reply, thinking block and tool call appears as it happens. The right pane shows the selected item in full: the command, the diff, the subagent's prompt and result. Each prompt shows its tokens, estimated cost and duration, and the header shows how full the context window is. Selecting a prompt shows where its turn's time went, in a waterfall where parallel calls overlap. Press x on an Agent call to expand its subagent's work inline, live while it runs. See the following guide for more.

heading: Watch every agent at once
body: The live board lists every session at work across your projects, with the ones waiting on you first. When a session asks for permission, the request appears in full under the list. Press A to allow it once, Y to always allow it, or D to deny it with a reason Claude sees. When a session's turn ends, press R to reply, and the agent carries on as if you'd typed it in its terminal. See the live board guide for more.

heading: Review and comment
body: The Diff tab shows what a session changed, either since the last commit or across its whole branch. Leave comments on a line, a range or a file, and press S to send them all to the agent, which picks them up mid-turn or keeps going after it finished. Replies, comments and answers to permission prompts reach the agent through Claude Code hooks, which you add once: See the review guide for more.

heading: Cost, files and time
body: The Stats tab breaks a session down by prompt, tool and model, and the Files tab lists every file it read or changed, each with its history as diffs. In the session picker, press s for totals across sessions and a daily cost chart, or f to find sessions by a file they changed, a command they ran or a prompt. See the cost and context guide for more.

heading: Alerts
body: While a session runs, the header flags a failed tool call, a stalled one, a finished turn, a compaction, a nearly full context or a permission request. With --notify , the same alerts arrive as desktop notifications through your terminal or the system, over SSH and in WSL too. With --cost-alert 5 and --long-turn 15m , a runaway session gets flagged as well. See the alerts reference for more.

heading: Copy and export
body: Press y to copy the selected command, diff or message, over SSH too, or e to export the timeline to Markdown. From the shell, snoop export writes the whole session to stdout. See the export guide for more.

heading: Notes
body: It reads the transcripts Claude Code already writes and sends nothing anywhere. The only change it makes to Claude Code's settings is the hooks, which snoop hooks uninstall removes. The transcript format is undocumented, and testing covers Claude Code 2.1.280 through 2.1.310. Unknown records are ignored, so a new version may show less rather than break, and an issue helps when something goes missing. A 75 MB transcript opens in about 150 ms. heading: Summary
body: ActionCache adds a caching layer to ASP.NET Core by annotating your endpoints. Cache a response, evict entries by namespace, or refresh cached actions with a single attribute — against an in-process or distributed backend, or several layered together.

heading: Why not [OutputCache] or HybridCache?
body: Fair question, and worth answering before you install anything. [OutputCache] HybridCache ActionCache --- --- --- --- Ships with ASP.NET Core Yes Yes (.NET 9+) No — a package Caches Full HTTP response Arbitrary values you fetch yourself Action/endpoint responses Attribute-driven Yes No — you call it in code Yes Stampede protection No Yes Yes L1 + L2 layering No Yes (memory + IDistributedCache ) Yes, and any number of layers Backends Memory, IDistributedCache Memory + IDistributedCache Memory, Redis, SQL Server , Cosmos DB Invalidate a group Tags Tags Namespaces, with route parameters ( Account:{id} ) Vary by caller VaryByValue (manual) Your key, your problem Automatic for authenticated requests Re-warm entries No No Yes — replays the recorded request Use [OutputCache] if it covers you. It is built in, costs no dependency, and needs no explanation to the next person who reads your code. Use HybridCache if you are caching values rather than responses, and want stampede protection and two-tier caching from the framework. Reach for ActionCache when you want attribute-driven response caching and something the other two don't do: eviction scoped to a route parameter, SQL Server or Cosmos as a backend, warming entries ahead of expiry, or per-user keys you don't have to remember to ask for.

heading: Features
body: Attribute-driven — add caching, eviction, or refresh to any endpoint with one attribute. Works with both MVC controllers and Minimal APIs . Four backends — in-process Memory , Redis , SQL Server , and Azure Cosmos DB , used individually or layered together. Namespaced eviction — group entries under a namespace (with route-parameter templates like Account:{id} ) and evict a whole namespace in one call. Cache refresh — replay the request recorded on each entry to warm it ahead of expiry. Fail-open by default — a backend outage degrades to a cache miss and logs a warning so requests still succeed; opt into fail-closed to propagate errors instead.

heading: Installation
body: ActionCache ships as one package per backend, so you only take the dependencies you use: Package Depends on --------- ------------ ActionCache ActionCache.Abstractions only — no Redis, SqlClient, Cosmos SDK or Newtonsoft ActionCache.Redis StackExchange.Redis ActionCache.SqlServer Microsoft.Data.SqlClient ActionCache.AzureCosmos Microsoft.Azure.Cosmos, Newtonsoft.Json ActionCache.Abstractions nothing — reference it to write a custom backend Configuration is unchanged: options.UseRedisCache(...) and friends still read the same, they just live in their own package now. Targets .NET 8 and .NET 10 .
